headline: Analysis and representation choices shape apparent findings in neuroimaging and brain-model evaluation
label: Neuroimaging Analysis Validity
summary: Three preprints show that parameterization, null models and prompt cues can drive apparent neuroimaging results, motivating stricter validation of analysis pipelines.
synthesis: The shared thread is that upstream representation and analysis decisions determine what neuroimaging results appear to show. The rich-club EEG study finds that null network construction and hub re-identification can create or erase apparent Alzheimer's group differences. The LLM connectivity-graph probe reports that ADHD predictions from rs-fMRI graphs follow class bias and prompt cues rather than subject-specific connectivity. The corpus callosum framework addresses representation directly, resampling the midsagittal callosum onto a standardized grid for diffusion MRI to avoid inter-subject misalignment. What is new is the emphasis on testing whether outputs depend on analysis choices or surface cues rather than on biological structure. All three are preprints, so the findings remain preliminary and unreplicated.
